title: Charging by electron transfer
keyIdea: When two insulators are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one to the other. The object that gains electrons becomes negatively charged; the object that loses them becomes positively charged by exactly the same amount. Positive charge does not move: protons stay in the nuclei of the atoms. No charge is made or destroyed, so the total charge stays zero. Charged objects then exert forces on each other: like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
familyTip: Rub a balloon on a wool jumper or dry hair and hold it near the hair: it pulls the strands up. Ask: which one gained electrons? (The balloon, so it is negative.) Then ask what the hair has now: the same amount of positive charge. Rub two balloons and hang them side by side; they push apart because both are negative. Watch for 'the hair gave the balloon positive charge'.

visual.caption: After rubbing, did each object gain or lose electrons? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: acetate rod rubbed with a cloth

lab.caption: Flagship lab: rub a balloon and count electrons, move charges by hand, give the equal and opposite charge, and predict forces.

kid: Everything is made of atoms. An atom has positive protons in its middle, called the nucleus. Negative electrons sit round the outside. Most things have the same number of each, so they have no charge.
Rub two things together and some electrons get pulled from one onto the other. The protons stay put. Only electrons move.
The thing that gains electrons now has more negative than positive. It is negative. The thing that loses them is positive by the same amount. If a balloon gains 3 electrons, the hair is +3.
No charge is made. It just moves, so the two charges add up to zero. Then the charged things push or pull. Two negative balloons push apart. A negative balloon and positive hair pull together.
adult: Ages 12 to 14. The KS3 physics programme of study in England covers 'separation of positive or negative charges when objects are rubbed together: transfer of electrons, forces between charged objects'. AQA GCSE Physics 4.2.5.1 then asks students to explain how insulators are charged by friction through electron transfer, and NGSS MS-PS2-3 and MS-PS2-5 cover electric forces and fields.

The physics: rubbing brings two surfaces into close contact and electrons transfer to the material that holds them more strongly (the triboelectric effect). Polythene rubbed with wool gains electrons and becomes negative; acetate or perspex rubbed with a cloth loses electrons and becomes positive. The charges are equal and opposite, so charge is conserved. Charge is measured in coulombs; each electron carries 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the lab counts whole electrons.

Common mistakes: saying positive charge or protons moved onto an object (a positive object has lost electrons), thinking rubbing creates charge, giving both objects the same sign, thinking the partner stays neutral, and expecting two like-charged balloons to attract. Students also mix up 'gains electrons' with 'becomes positive', because gaining sounds like adding something good.

In the lab your child rubs a balloon on hair and watches 3 electrons hop across while both charges and the total are shown, drags charges between a rod and a cloth (a proton refuses to move), gives the partner's charge in three cases, works out the direction of electron flow from four material clues, and predicts attract or repel for four pairs.

practice.prompt: A balloon rubbed on hair becomes negatively charged. What happened?
choices: Electrons moved from the hair to the balloon
Protons moved from the balloon to the hair
practice.hint: Only one kind of particle can be rubbed off a surface.
practice.explain: Electrons transfer from the hair to the balloon, so the balloon has extra electrons and is negative. Protons stay in the nuclei.

practice.prompt: A polythene rod gains {n} electrons from a wool cloth. What is the charge on the cloth, counted in electron charges? (Write a positive number for a positive charge.)
practice.hint: The cloth lost exactly the electrons the rod gained.
practice.explain: The cloth lost {n} electrons, so it has {n} more protons than electrons: +{n}.

practice.prompt: An acetate rod is positive after rubbing with a cloth. What charge does the cloth have?
practice.hint: Where did the acetate's electrons go?
practice.explain: The cloth gained the electrons the rod lost, so it is negative by the same amount.

practice.prompt: Before rubbing, a rod and a cloth each have charge 0. After rubbing, the rod is −{n}. What is the total charge of the rod and cloth together?
practice.hint: Rubbing moves charge. It does not make or destroy it.
practice.explain: The cloth is +{n}, and −{n} + {n} = 0. Charge is conserved.

practice.prompt: Two balloons are both rubbed on the same hair and hung side by side. What happens?
practice.hint: Both gained electrons. What sign does each have?
practice.explain: Both are negative. Like charges repel, so they push apart.

pool.prompt: Why can rubbing move electrons but not protons?
choices: Protons are held in the nucleus; outer electrons can be pulled off
Protons are too heavy to see
pool.hint: Think about where each particle sits in an atom.
pool.explain: Protons are bound in the nucleus. Electrons on the outside of surface atoms can be transferred by rubbing.

pool.prompt: A rod becomes positive. Which statement is right?
pool.hint: Positive means fewer electrons than protons.
pool.explain: The rod has fewer electrons than protons because it lost electrons. No protons moved.

pool.prompt: A cloth ends up with a charge of −{n} electron charges after rubbing a perspex rod. What is the size of the charge on the rod?
pool.hint: The rod lost what the cloth gained: equal size, opposite sign.
pool.explain: The rod lost the {n} electrons the cloth gained, so it is +{n}: the same size, opposite sign.

pool.prompt: A negative polythene rod is brought near a positive acetate rod. They ...
pool.hint: One rod is negative and one is positive: opposite charges.
pool.explain: Negative and positive are opposite charges, so they attract.

pool.prompt: Which sentence about charging by rubbing is true?
choices: Charge is made by the rubbing
Charge is destroyed by the rubbing
pool.hint: Add the two charges after rubbing.
pool.explain: The two charges are equal and opposite and add to zero, so charge is only moved.

pool.prompt: A balloon has {p} protons and gains {g} electrons from hair. It started neutral. How many electrons does it have now?
pool.hint: Neutral means as many electrons as protons. Then add the ones it gained.
pool.explain: It started with {p} electrons and gained {g}, so {=p+g}. Its charge is −{g}.

pool.prompt: Which way do electrons move when a polythene rod is rubbed with wool and becomes negative?
choices: From the wool to the rod
From the rod to the wool
pool.hint: Which one ends up with extra electrons?
pool.explain: The rod is negative, so it gained electrons from the wool.

pool.prompt: A student says: 'The hair gave the balloon its negative charge, so the hair is now neutral.' What is wrong?
choices: The hair lost electrons, so it is now positive
The hair is now negative too
pool.hint: What does losing electrons do to an object's charge?
pool.explain: Losing electrons leaves the hair with more protons than electrons, so it is positive by the same amount.

pool.prompt: Two objects are rubbed. One ends up −{n}. How many electrons were transferred?
pool.explain: A charge of −{n} means {n} extra electrons, so {n} were transferred.

pool.prompt: Why does a charged balloon pull charged hair towards it?
pool.hint: The balloon is negative. What is the hair?
pool.explain: The balloon is negative and the hair is positive. Opposite charges attract.
